author: haiku
reason: B gives an engineer new to the project a simpler runtime path to follow: each attempt starts over, the table schema is listed in full, and it explains the reasons behind its thresholds. A's checkpoints, leases, heartbeats and continuation jobs spread state and failure handling across many interlocking steps, so it takes longer to understand correctly.

author: haiku
reason: Both documents use the same per-step structure (what starts it, what moves, state, failure), but A is easier to follow: each attempt restarts from scratch and state lives in one plainly described table, while B adds leases, heartbeats, checkpoints and continuation jobs, which makes its failure paths harder to trace correctly.

author: sonnet
reason: B is easier for a newcomer to follow: it opens with a plain overview, explains what a multipart upload is, and maps each step to the small or large path, while A's step 3 is confusing because its sub-steps also say "go to step 4", mixing sub-step and step numbers, even though A has a useful failure table.

author: sonnet
reason: A opens with a short two-path overview and a map of which steps belong to which path, then labels every step the same way, so an outsider can follow the flow faster. B packs more of the existing-system context and the repair logic into a dense terms section and nested conditionals before the flow starts.

author: haiku
reason: A sets out the flow as numbered steps that say what triggers each one and where its data lives, and it gathers every failure case into one table, so a newcomer can follow the whole path quickly; B spreads the same behaviour across diagram notes, design decisions and script notes, and adds side issues such as replica failover and the gateway-versus-Redis clock difference that slow down understanding.

author: haiku
reason: B is easier to follow: its numbered steps say what starts each step and where data is kept, a failure table covers each failure case, and its diagram shows the local cache plainly, while A spreads the same flow across design-decision bullets and a script the reader has to piece together.

author: sonnet
reason: Document A is easier to follow: a clean diagram, short notes on how the counter works, and a single table that maps each failure to its outcome, while B packs the script's steps and the headers into the diagram and spreads the failure behaviour across many prose notes.

author: sonnet
reason: B is the faster read for an outsider: it first describes the existing gateway and Key Service, then shows a numbered diagram, then gathers every failure case in one table with a worked Retry-After example, while A spreads the same mechanics across a dense diagram and many separate notes.

author: haiku
reason: A writes out every switch step concretely in the same starts/does/state/fails format, around one write-state flag and one copy rule; B makes the reader map a generic procedure S, plus control rows and epochs, onto each direction, including an awkward Postgres-to-Postgres case, which takes longer to understand correctly.

author: haiku
reason: B is easier to follow. It starts with a plain summary, it runs on one named write-state flag with five values, it has a table of where state lives, and it spells out each pause, drain and flip step inline. A relies on an abstract procedure S built from control rows, epochs, fencing and step-skipping (for example, running S with Postgres as both old and new source), which the reader has to keep in mind and cross-reference.

author: sonnet
reason: B gives a three-part summary of the write path (commit with outbox, quick copy, drainer repair) at the start, explains how the fence works mechanically, and groups the checklist into named phases, so a newcomer understands it sooner. A packs dense detail into its definitions and uses a confusing three-state fence, even though its state and failure tables are useful.

author: sonnet
reason: A opens with a short three-part mechanism (commit with outbox, quick copy, drainer repair) that runs in both directions, then gives every step the same Starts/Changes/State/If-it-fails fields. B's state and failure tables are useful, but its mechanism is spread across more sections and side concerns such as the fence modes, the deferred unique email index and the staging step, so a newcomer would build an accurate picture faster from A.

author: haiku
reason: A is quicker to follow and harder to misread: every mode uses the same Starts/Does/Gate/When-it-goes-wrong layout, there is one numbered rollback sequence with a single claim-before-charge ownership rule, and failures sit in one table, while B splits rollback into two parallel paths and its diagram puts each step's description on the arrow leaving that step.

author: haiku
reason: B is quicker to follow: each mode lists what starts it, what it does and how it can fail, rollback is one ordered sequence with a single branch for new_only, and failures sit in one table, while A repeats the rollback steps across its diagram, list and safety rules and blurs where rollback ends (old_only or shadow).

author: sonnet
reason: B is longer, but it spells out each rollback path, what reconciliation does for every period, where the rollback step lives and how workers check it before every charge, so an engineer gets the mechanism right; A is faster to read but vague on reconciliation and charge safety, and has small inconsistencies such as "steps 3 is skipped" and a "halt" step from shadow that has nothing to halt.

author: sonnet
reason: Document A is clearer because its diagram, its numbered rollback steps and its per-path step lists all agree, and it says exactly where the rollback state lives and how double charges are blocked; Document B's diagram and text disagree on step order (Reconcile before Reprocess in the diagram, a fifth Commit step only in the text, and shadow going through the full rollback), which leaves a newcomer unsure what actually happens.

author: haiku
reason: B gives the four possible outcomes first, then a short numbered flow in plain words, then a diagram with labelled boxes and mostly straight paths, so a newcomer understands it faster than A, whose diagram sends refund outcomes back through the charge webhook decision and whose steps branch into 6a, 6b and 6c.

author: haiku
reason: A opens with the four possible outcomes, then gives a short numbered flow and a diagram whose edges match that flow exactly, so the steps are easy to follow; B's diagram has confusing edges (refund outcomes coming out of the charge-outcome decision, PAY_REF looping back to the provider) and more storage detail, both of which slow a newcomer down.

author: sonnet
reason: B makes Order the coordinator from the start, shows what the customer sees in its own lane, and ends with a status tree and a failure table that settle each failure branch, so a newcomer can work out triggers, state and failures faster than from A, whose notes depend more on the diagram.

author: sonnet
reason: Document A is easier to follow: it opens with a one-sentence summary, names each service's tables in the diagram, labels every arrow as HTTP or event, and adds a status tree and a failure table, so an engineer can see what triggers each step, where state lives and how each failure ends. In B some flows end loosely: Refunded never reaches Order, and the expiry timer is not connected to anything.

author: haiku
reason: A is quicker to take in: a one-paragraph summary, a single route stamp fixed at enqueue, one table of where state lives and one table of failures give the whole picture at a glance, while B adds a three-state owner machine, an ambiguity rule and a stuck threshold it never defines, all inside dense invariants.

author: haiku
reason: B opens with a plain summary and a "how the system works" overview, then adds a state-location table and a single failure table, so a newcomer sees the whole flow before the steps; A starts with dense invariants that point forward to later sections, and its three-state ownership model and ambiguity rules take longer to piece together.

author: sonnet
reason: A shows the runtime as one numbered pipeline (record, hand off, store, send, page, report back, alarm), backed by an ownership table and a single failure table, so a newcomer sees what triggers each step, where state lives and how failures play out in one place; B spreads those mechanics across its rollout steps and adds extra publishing/published lease states, though it defines its terms more carefully.

author: sonnet
reason: B gives the whole runtime path in one numbered flow (record, hand off, store, send, page, report back, alarm), with an ownership-by-status table and a single failure table, while A spreads the mechanism across a component list and rollout steps 3 and 4 and adds the extra publishing/published lease states.
